Empirical Research Plan  
“Imports from China, Innovation, IT Adoption, and Productivity in UK Firms (1996–2007)”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy:  Two-way fixed-effects difference-in-differences (DiD) at the
firm-year level, instrumenting the within-industry time-varying treatment
(Chinese import penetration) with a shift–share (Bartik) instrument.

Why appropriate?  
•  Timing: China’s WTO entry in 2001 produced a sharp, plausibly
exogenous supply-side shock.  
•  Cross-section: Exposure differs across 4-digit SIC industries because
1996 pre-WTO UK spending patterns varied.  
•  Shift–share IV removes the remaining endogeneity of UK
industry-specific demand shocks by using Chinese export growth in other
high-income markets as the shifter, interacted with the UK’s
predetermined 1996 industry mix.

Main estimating equation (second stage)

Y_it = β · ImportPen_it  + γ_i + δ_{s,t} + ϕ_t + X′_{it} θ + ε_it

where  
Y_it   = patents, log(IT capital), or TFP of firm i in year t  
ImportPen_it = Chinese import penetration in i’s 4-digit industry s in
year t (instrumented)  
γ_i    = firm fixed effects  
δ_{s,t}= industry–year fixed effects (captures common technology shocks)  
ϕ_t    = year dummies (macro shocks)  
X_it   = time-varying controls (size, exporter status, R&D tax credits)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
ImportPen_it = (Chinese imports to the UK in industry s at t)
/ (UK domestic absorption in industry s at t).  
Scale in %-points or SD units.

Treatment definition  
“High-exposure” firms: above-median cumulative ΔImportPen between 2001
and 2007.  
“Low-exposure” firms: below-median industries (counterfactual).

Timing  
Pre-period: 1996–2000  
Post-treatment: 2001–2007  
The intensity varies continuously; DiD exploits both the step-change in
2001 and heterogeneous slopes thereafter.

Shift–share instrument  
Predetermined shares: UK industry absorption shares in 1996.  
Shifter: growth of Chinese exports to all other OECD countries in the
same 4-digit industry, excluding the UK.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1 Parallel Trends (conditional)  
Absent the Chinese shock, outcomes of high- and low-exposure firms would
have followed similar trends.  
Plausibility:  testable via pre-1996–2000 event-study; industry-year FE
absorb shared shocks.

A2 Exogeneity of Shift–Share Shifter  
Chinese export growth to other countries is driven by China-specific
supply factors, not UK-specific demand.  
Plausibility:  widely used in trade literature; exclude EU partners to
minimise correlated demand.

A3 Stable Industry Assignment  
Firms’ 4-digit SIC remains constant or changes exogenously.  
Plausibility:  UK reclassification rare; we will fix industry at 1996 or
instrument at that level and test robustness excluding switchers.

A4 No General-Equilibrium Spillovers that Violate SUTVA  
One firm’s treatment does not mechanically alter another’s potential
outcome outside its industry.  
Plausibility:  Some spillovers via supply chains; partially addressed by
industry-year FE and robustness dropping highly interconnected
industries.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1 Endogenous Import Demand Shocks  
• UK consumers may demand more Chinese goods where domestic firms were
already stagnating.  
Remedy:  IV with external export growth; include UK import demand from
all other countries as control.

T2 Differential Pre-Trends in Technology Trajectories  
• Advanced industries might both innovate more and face more Chinese
imports.  
Remedy:  (i) event-study plot of β_τ for τ<0; (ii) include lagged outcome
levels; (iii) match on 1996 innovation levels and run matched-DiD.

T3 Firm Selection / Exit  
• Low-productivity firms may exit after import surge, biasing results on
survivors.  
Remedy:  (i) inverse-probability-weighted estimators for survival;
(ii) re-estimate including exited firms with outcomes set to zero after
exit; (iii) Heckman selection correction as robustness.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dim FE and IV
library(multiwayvcov)
library(lmtest)
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data -----------------------------------------------------------
firm <- fread("uk_firm_panel_1996_2007.csv")       # firm-level outcomes
imports <- fread("uk_china_imports_4digit.csv")    # imports by ind-year
absorb  <- fread("uk_domestic_absorption.csv")     # absorption by ind-year
exports_other <- fread("china_exports_oecd.csv")   # shifter

# 2. Construct treatment -------------------------------------------------
# a) Import penetration
imports[, imp_pen := china_imports / domestic_absorption]
firm <- merge(firm, imports[, .(industry4, year, imp_pen)], 
              by = c("industry4","year"), all.x = TRUE)

# b) Shift–share instrument
# Predetermined UK shares in 1996
base_share <- absorb[year == 1996, .(industry4, share96 = domestic_absorption/
                                                     sum(domestic_absorption))]
# National-level shifter (exclude UK)
exports_other[, growth := log(china_exports) - log(shift(china_exports)), 
              by = industry4]
ss <- merge(base_share, exports_other[, .(industry4, year, growth)],
            by = "industry4")
ss[, bartik := share96 * growth]
firm <- merge(firm, ss[, .(industry4, year, bartik)], 
              by = c("industry4","year"), all.x = TRUE)

# 3. Controls & Outcomes -------------------------------------------------
firm[, log_tfp := log(TFP)]
firm[, log_it  := log(IT_investment + 1)]
firm[, patents  := patent_count]

# 4. Main IV specification ----------------------------------------------
spec <- feols(log_tfp ~ 1 | firm_id + industry4^year + year | imp_pen ~ bartik,
              data = firm, 
              cluster = ~industry4)

summary(spec)

# 5. Robustness: event-study --------------------------------------------
firm[, post01 := (year >= 2001)]
for(lag in -5:5) firm[, paste0("event_",lag) := as.numeric(year - 2001 == lag)]

event_formula <- as.formula(
  paste("log_tfp ~", paste(paste0("event_", -5:5), collapse = " + "),
        "| firm_id + industry4^year + year"))
event <- feols(event_formula, data = firm, cluster = ~industry4)
iplot(event)  # pre-trend visualisation
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results (Priors)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory (Schumpeterian “escape-competition” models) and empirical
evidence (e.g., Bloom et al. 2016) suggest:

• Sign: β > 0  
• Magnitude (back-of-the-envelope): A one-SD (≈4-pp) rise in Chinese
import penetration raises patents by 6 %, IT capital by 3 %, and TFP by
1-1.5 % within five years.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Relevance of Instrument (F-stat > 10):        1  
2. Exogeneity of Instrument/Shock:               0.8  
3. Parallel Trends in Pre-Period:                0.9  
4. No Spillovers/SUTVA:                          0.7  
5. Stable Composition (no differential exit):    0.8  

Overall credibility ≈ 4.2 / 5.
